brief.goal: Find the two poles of a magnet and predict when two magnets pull together or push apart

big_idea.text: A magnet has two pole ends: unlike poles pull together, while like poles push apart.

why_it_matters.text: You can use the push or pull between labelled magnet ends to work out how magnets will move before they touch.

the_why.text: Iron filings collect mainly at a bar magnet's two ends, showing the special regions called poles. When facing ends are unlike, the magnets move toward one another; when they are alike, they move apart.

objectives.can: Locate the two pole regions of a bar magnet from where iron filings gather.
Predict whether two labelled magnet ends will pull together or push apart.
Tell apart a permanent magnet from an iron bar by using repulsion as evidence.
Explain the attraction-or-repulsion prediction using whether the facing poles are alike or unlike.

picture.text: Start with one horizontal bar magnet under a sheet of paper, with a small scatter of iron filings. The filings gather densely at the two ends and scarcely in the middle; label the ends N and S. Keep this same bar magnet on pencil rollers, then slide a second labelled bar magnet toward its right end: first show S facing N with inward arrows, then show N facing N with outward arrows.
picture.standard: Iron-filings pole demonstration followed by two bar magnets on rolling pencils

needs_first.text: Recognise the two ends and the middle of a bar-shaped object.
Understand that an arrow can show an object's direction of movement.

mistakes.mistake: Iron filings stick equally all along a bar magnet.
mistakes.why_it_fails: The filings gather most densely near the two ends, not uniformly along the magnet.

mistakes.mistake: Any two magnets will always attract.
mistakes.why_it_fails: Only unlike facing poles attract; two North poles or two South poles repel.

mistakes.mistake: If an iron bar is attracted to a magnet, it must itself be a permanent magnet.
mistakes.why_it_fails: Both ends of an iron bar are attracted to either pole, whereas repulsion is the useful evidence that the other object is a magnet.

mistakes.mistake: A magnet can be broken to leave one North pole alone or one South pole alone.
mistakes.why_it_fails: Each smaller piece still has both a North pole and a South pole.

opening_question.question: Two bar magnets are brought close end to end. Will they always pull together, or could they sometimes push apart? Commit to a guess.
guesses: They might push apart when the same kinds of ends face.
They will do nothing until they touch.
opening_question.answer: They pull together when unlike poles face and push apart when like poles face.

route.what: Show two unlabelled-looking coloured bar magnets approaching end to end and ask whether every pair must pull together or whether one arrangement could push apart.
Pause beside three possible motions—together, apart, or no movement—so the learner chooses before seeing the test.
Sprinkle and tap iron filings above one bar magnet. Animate many filings gathering at each end and only a few at the middle; ask where the magnet seems strongest.
Ask why the ends deserve attention rather than the middle; answer that the filings crowd at the ends, so these are the special interaction regions.
Add N to one crowded end and S to the other, naming these two ends poles. Briefly show a snapped bar becoming two smaller N–S magnets to break the single-pole idea.
Place magnet A across pencil rollers. Bring magnet B's S end toward A's N end; ask for a prediction, then animate A rolling toward B without touching it.
Keep magnet A and the pencils unchanged, but turn magnet B so N faces N. Ask what changes, then animate A rolling away. State the side-by-side rule: unlike poles attract; like poles repel.
Give three facing-end pairs—S–N, N–N, and S–S—and ask the learner to decide pull or push, including an iron-bar case that tests the idea that attraction alone proves a magnet.
The learner uses paper pole cards to predict and sort pull and push pairings, then says the reason aloud.
Return to the opening magnets and ask the learner to complete: “I look at the two facing poles; if they are ___, the magnets ___.”

questions.question: After iron filings are sprinkled above a bar magnet, where should most of them collect?
questions.explain: The filings gather most at the ends, showing where the magnet's poles are.

questions.question: Magnet A has its N end facing magnet B's N end. What should magnet A do on its pencil rollers?
options: Stay still because magnets act only after touching
questions.explain: N and N are like poles, and like poles repel.

questions.question: A bar magnet attracts both ends of an unmarked metal bar. What can you decide from that observation?
options: It might be an iron bar, so attraction alone does not prove it is a magnet
It must be a magnet because it is attracted
It has only a North pole
questions.explain: Iron is attracted by either pole; observing repulsion is what identifies another magnet.

try_it.title: Pole-pair prediction cards
try_it.stands_for: Each paper strip is one bar magnet; its two labelled ends stand for its North and South poles.
try_it.predict: Before moving the strips, predict: if N faces N, will the pair pull or push?
steps: Write N at one end and S at the other end of each strip.
Place the strips so N faces N, and write PULL or PUSH before changing them.
Turn one strip so N faces S, and write PULL or PUSH.
Say the reason for both predictions aloud.
try_it.observe: Your completed pairings show N–N and S–S as PUSH, while N–S and S–N are PULL.
try_it.question: Why does turning one paper magnet change a push prediction into a pull prediction?
try_it.expected: Turning one strip changes the facing pair from like poles to unlike poles. Real magnets with like poles repel, so N facing N would push; real magnets with unlike poles attract, so N facing S would pull.
try_it.write:
“N facing N gives a push because the poles are alike.”
“N facing S gives a pull because the poles are unlike.”
try_it.in_class: Pairs make two labelled paper strips. The teacher writes “N–N ___; N–S ___; S–S ___” on the board. Ask, “Which facing pair would push, and why?” A class that writes PULL for N–N is treating all magnets as always attracting.

leave_out: Magnetic and non-magnetic materials, except for the brief iron-bar contrast used to show why attraction alone is not proof of a magnet.
A freely suspended magnet, Earth’s magnetic behaviour, and compass navigation.
Magnetic effects through wood, plastic, or glass.
Atomic, electron, and quantum explanations of magnetism.
How to make, store, or maintain magnets.

from_lectures.took: Use the iron-filings or nails observation to make the two ends visible before naming them poles, then use a short prediction check.
from_lectures.left: Compass direction, barriers, and broad material classification are omitted because the lesson focuses tightly on poles and pair interactions.

from_lectures.took: Use the central contrast of two bar magnets on pencil rollers: one unlike-pole pair moves together and one like-pole pair moves apart.
from_lectures.left: The compass and barrier extension are omitted so there is time for the learner to predict both contrasting cases and explain the rule.

from_lectures.took: Keep the productive opening puzzle that magnets may either pull or push, rather than treating magnetism as only attraction.
from_lectures.left: The quantum account of electrons, wave functions, and virtual photons is far beyond a foundation Class 6 lesson and does not help this lesson's observable pole predictions.
